findings.location: sections/50-comparison.tex, first paragraph, final sentence (PDF p. 31): "All three hear the orations as prayer rather than as the anchors of an argument, and call on the Council of Trent for the doctrine of the sacrament those prayers ask to receive."
findings.problem: The claim is false of the second reading. 'Trent' and 'Tridentin' occur nowhere in sections/30-son-and-lord-of-david.tex; that reading's treatment of the orations (its 'The other texts as confession' subsection) rests on the Secret's maiestas, the Preface's concluding clause and the Postcommunion's sanctificationes, and cites no council. Only sections/20-whole-heart-one-body.tex (Trent as the sign of the one body) and sections/40-just-judge-merciful-hearer.tex (Trent as the antidote against daily faults) call on it. The research record's own comparison, research/interpretations.md 4.1, is looser ('use Trent only as doctrinal illumination'), but the study has turned that into a positive assertion about all three. The comparison section exists to state truly what the readings share, and a reader who checks the second reading finds the shared feature absent.
findings.required_result: The comparison states what the three readings actually share about the orations. Either restrict the Trent sentence to the readings that use it (the first and the third), or drop the clause and keep the true half ('All three hear the orations as prayer rather than as the anchors of an argument'). Do not add a Trent citation to the second reading merely to make the sentence true.

findings.location: sections/80-date-location.tex, Gospel dossier (PDF p. 33): Location cell 'Event: the Temple, Jerusalem (21:23); place of writing not recorded' and explanatory row 'No first audience is recorded.'
findings.problem: The dossier rule this appendix answers requires, for each passage, the author or compositional horizon, the first audience, and the composition place beside the date, and requires writer, event and recipient geography to be distinguished; the Gospel's dossier supplies none of the three. The Epistle's dossier does it correctly in the same table ('at Rome or Caesarea; to the saints at Ephesus (1:1)', with the Ephesian gentiles named in the explanatory row), so the omission is not a house convention but a gap. It is not a limit of the chronology corpus either: only dates must come from the corpus, and the Catholic Encyclopedia article already bound and read for the Gospel's six traditional ranges (Jacquier, 'Gospel of St. Matthew', vol. 10, 1911, whose lines 201 and 203 research/scope.md 7.3 records reading) carries the traditional audience and place of composition. The research records hold neither: a search of research/scope.md and research/context.md for an audience, a place of writing or Palestine returns nothing for Matthew, and 3.6 records only literary context and reception. The defect matters beyond this page, because guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md makes this appendix the reviewed home of the chronology the concise study's physical page 2 reprints, so the gap is inherited by a document that cannot introduce a new source-dependent claim of its own.
findings.required_result: research/scope.md records, at its own locus in the already-bound Catholic Encyclopedia article on Matthew (and, for the Offertory, in the bound article on Daniel), the traditional first audience and place of composition, kept distinct from the narrated event's place and from the modern critical horizon; sections/80-date-location.tex then carries them in the Gospel dossier as the Epistle dossier already carries its own, so that no appointed passage's dossier reports a required field as simply not recorded. No date, era or reign may be added from these articles: every figure still reaches the Date cell only through the generated chronology annotations.

findings.location: sections/20-whole-heart-one-body.tex, 'Two commandments, one love' (PDF p. 14): "One of his homilies on the Gospels expounds the parable that stands just before this Gospel in Matthew, the king's wedding feast (Mt 22:1--13)."
findings.problem: The wedding feast does not stand just before this Gospel. Two pericopes intervene, as the study's own Gospel section says nine pages earlier: 'the tribute to Caesar (22:15--22), the Sadducees' question about the resurrection (22:23--33), and now the Pharisees'. The research record is careful here and says only that Gregory's homily is on 'the pericope that precedes this Gospel in Mt 22'. Nothing in the argument turns on it -- Gregory's contribution is correctly presented as doctrinal reception of the double commandment cited from Mk 12:30, not as exegesis of Mt 22:34--46 -- but the sentence contradicts the study elsewhere and a reader who follows the chapter will notice.
findings.required_result: The sentence places Gregory's parable accurately in Matthew 22, for example 'the parable that opens the same chapter' or 'the parable of the king's wedding feast earlier in Matthew 22', without disturbing the correct statement that Gregory expounds the parable and cites the commandment from Mark.

findings.location: sections/30-son-and-lord-of-david.tex, end of 'By the word of the Lord and the spirit of his mouth' (PDF p. 23): "The Trinitarian sense of the verse is the Fathers' reading and not a signal of the page."
findings.problem: The sentence tells the reader that the study has declined to press an inference from the Missal's typography. That register belongs to the audit record, where research/interpretations.md 2.5 already holds it, and not to the body: a constraint on what may be asserted is met by not asserting it. It also leaves the paragraph arguing against itself, since the lower-case spiritu is introduced only to be set aside while the votive Mass's capital is offered as evidence of how the same book read the verse. This is the one sentence of its kind in the study, which is otherwise disciplined about stating findings rather than the restraint behind them, so it does not amount to the recurring habit the editorial standard treats as a failure.
findings.required_result: The paragraph states the typographic facts and the Fathers' reading of Ps 32:6 directly, without a sentence whose subject is what the study does or declines to conclude from the printing.

findings.location: proper-components.toml, [[lanes]] key = "son-and-lord-of-david", authors list; against sections/30-son-and-lord-of-david.tex (PDF pp. 21 and 24), which develops Theodoret of Cyrus twice
findings.problem: The second reading names Theodoret twice and gives him substantive work -- 'Theodoret of Cyrus names the same three relations lordship, providence and indwelling', and again in 'The difficulties this confession must carry', where he stands with Chrysostom against the distribution of Eph 4:6 among the Persons -- but the manifest's author list for that lane omits him, and research/interpretations.md 2.6 says flatly that he 'is not one of this reading's witnesses'. The prose use is correct and does not credit him with the distribution; the manifest and the record simply no longer describe the section as written.
findings.required_result: The lane record and the prose agree: either add Theodoret to the son-and-lord-of-david lane's authors and adjust research/interpretations.md 2.6 to say how he is used there, or attribute the three relations in that section to Chrysostom alone and leave Theodoret to the first reading, where the manifest already carries him.

summary: Cold review of the expansive study liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost (main.tex, nine sections, 37 physical pages, within the 20-50 range), read whole against propers/verified.md, research/scope.md, research/interpretations.md, research/chronology-annotations.tex, guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md and the 1962 profile; the nineteen sealed files were re-hashed and match REVIEW_INPUTS. Independently checked: all ten Latin proper texts against the collation (exact match, element for element); Gregory Hom. in Ev. 38 in the tracked Wikisource Latin (pericope heading Mt 22:1-13, 'sicut in duobus lignis', 'qui sibi de se nihil relinquit', the commandment cited from Mk 12:30); eight Bellarmine quotations in the tracked O'Sullivan text, each in its own psalm's place; Schuster's Good Friday processional-psalm claim in the tracked volume-3 OCR. The three readings are genuinely distinguishable, each engages all ten elements, each carries four real senses in which neither the literal nor the anagogical collapses into the moral, and each develops reasoning from well over two checked Fathers; the attribution discipline is unusually good (Gregory expounding the parable and not this pericope, Irenaeus using Ps 32:6 as a proof-text and not expounding it, Rupert and Durandus confined to the chants of an office whose Gospel was Luke 14, the two lines of exegesis at Eph 4:6 kept apart). Two blocking defects remain: the comparison asserts a Trent citation the second reading does not make, and the Scriptural Date and Location dossier leaves the Gospel without the first audience and place of composition its owning profile requires, in the very appendix the concise page 2 will reprint. Limits of this review: patristic and medieval sources not tracked in this checkout (Jerome PL 26, Chrysostom NPNF, Cassiodorus, Hilary CSEL 22, Theodoret PG 82, Rupert, Durandus, Wilson's sacramentaries, the Sextuplex view) were audited against the leaf's own records and their internal consistency, not re-read at their loci; the mechanical gates (check-content-preflight, all twelve checks, and provenance-matches-run) pass and were not re-derived. A third-party note, not a finding: the Offertory's generated Date cell prints 'Historical setting: Duration: all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years', a chronology-corpus projection the study may not hand-edit and which research/scope.md 7.4 has already reported to the corpus owner.
